name: WALL-E (2008)
teaser: Pixar made a feature with the first 40 minutes having no dialogue. The opening is a 40-minute love story between two robots and a cockroach. The film won Pixar its second Best Picture nomination.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch with no commentary. The first 40 minutes is gesture, sound, and the machines' reading of human artifacts. Pixar was betting that cinema can sustain a feature without dialogue — and they were right.

name: Up (2009)
teaser: Pixar's opening montage is the most-deconstructed 9 minutes in animation history. They tested it on the toughest crowd they had and still made it 20 seconds longer. Children sat silently for the whole thing.

exploreAction.targetName: Up (2009) — opening montage to end of opening credits (11 min)
exploreAction.instruction: Watch carefully. The opening montage tells a 60-year love story in 9 minutes without a single line of dialogue. They tested this with the most distracted audience at Pixar — children — and the kids sat still for the whole thing.

name: Soul (2020)
teaser: Pixar's film — a jazz pianist who dies before his big break and must help a reluctant soul find its 'spark' — won the Oscars for Best Animated Feature and Best Original Score (Jon Batiste and Trent Reznor). It became Pixar's most philosophical film: the argument, delivered through a Manhattan music teacher and a lost soul named 22, is that the 'spark' isn't a purpose — it's the willingness to live.

exploreAction.targetName: Soul (2020) — the Great Before and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Joe's rehearsal, the phone call, the manhole — and notice how the film's two worlds are set: the real New York, photographed with texture and music, and the Great Before, designed as a blue abstract.

name: Coco (2017)
teaser: The 'Remember Me' twist is the film's heart: a lullaby disguised as a pop song, and the truth about who really wrote it. Pixar built the Land of the Dead from real Mexican artisans' work and spent years researching Día de los Muertos — the marigold bridge was their hardest technical challenge. It's the rare film that makes you cry twice: once for family, once for memory.

exploreAction.targetName: Coco (2017) — the opening and the Remember Me scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the papel picado prologue, then the final Remember Me performance. Notice how the song's meaning flips completely once you know who really wrote it — and how the marigold bridge is both a visual and an emotional threshold.

name: The Little Mermaid (1989)
teaser: The film that saved Disney animation — after a decade of decline, this underwater fairy tale about a mermaid who trades her voice for legs launched the 'Disney Renaissance' and changed the industry. Howard Ashman's songs ('Part of Your World,' 'Under the Sea') and the villain Ursula made it a musical first, and its box office ($211 million) proved animation could rival live action. It was the first animated film with a Broadway-style score.

exploreAction.targetName: The Little Mermaid (1989) — the 'Part of Your World' scene and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Part of Your World' sequence — Ariel's grotto, the treasures, the longing — and notice how the song establishes the film's theme in one number: the desire to be part of the human world is the whole story, and the animation (the underwater movement was a technical breakthrough) sells every note.

name: Beauty and the Beast (1991)
teaser: The first animated film ever nominated for Best Picture — Disney's fairy tale with the most ambitious animation ever attempted (the ballroom scene was the first extensive use of CGI in a feature). The songs by Alan Menken and the late Howard Ashman ('Be Our Guest,' 'Belle,' and the title song that won the Oscar) made it a musical masterpiece, and its 'Tale as Old as Time' ballroom dance is the most romantic sequence in animation.

exploreAction.targetName: Beauty and the Beast (1991) — the ballroom scene and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ballroom sequence — the gown, the dance, the computer-animated camera sweep — and notice how the film's technology serves its emotion: the CGI camera move (the first of its kind) makes the dance feel like a dream, and the song's lyrics ('Tale as Old as Time') are the film's thesis.

name: Aladdin (1992)
teaser: The most purely entertaining of the Disney Renaissance — Robin Williams' Genie, whose improvised, pop-culture-saturated performance rewrote what animation voice acting could be, and the film's 'A Whole New World' (the first Disney song to hit #1). The animation (the 'Never Had a Friend Like Me' number is a showcase) and the film's $504 million gross made it the year's biggest hit.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Friend Like Me' number — the Genie's shapeshifting showcase, the chorus, the pure animation virtuosity — and notice how Williams' improvisation drives the sequence: the animators worked from his audio tracks, and the result is the most energetic scene in Disney history.

name: The Lion King (1994)
teaser: The highest-grossing animated film of its era and the most beloved of the Disney Renaissance — Hamlet with lions, Elton John's songs, and the most famous death scene in animation (Mufasa's stampede). The film's 'Circle of Life' opening, its 'Hakuna Matata,' and its 'Can You Feel the Love Tonight' (which won the Oscar) made it a cultural constant, and its 1994 gross ($763 million) was a record for an animated film. It ran on Broadway for 25 years.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lion King (1994) — the stampede and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the stampede sequence — the wildebeests, Mufasa's fall, Simba's 'Dad, wake up' — and notice how the film earns its grief: the animation (a stampede of millions of wildebeests) was a technical milestone, and the scene's silence after the roar is the film's emotional core.

name: Toy Story (1995)
teaser: The first feature film made entirely on computers — Pixar's story of a cowboy doll (Tom Hanks) jealous of the new spaceman (Tim Allen) changed animation forever. John Lasseter's film proved CGI could carry emotion, and its box office ($373 million) launched the most successful animation studio in history.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film's opening act — Andy's room, the toys' secret life, Woody's jealousy — and notice how the film's technology serves the story: the toys' limited movement (the first CGI had to work within plastic logic) became character, and the animation's warmth was a breakthrough.

name: Finding Nemo (2003)
teaser: Pixar's ocean epic — a clownfish father (Albert Brooks) crosses the Pacific to rescue his son, with a forgetful blue tang (Ellen DeGeneres's Dory) as his guide. The film's rendering of water — the most difficult animation challenge of its era — won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, and its 'P. Sherman, 42 Wallaby Way, Sydney' became a global catchphrase. It grossed $940 million, making it the best-selling DVD of all time.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film's first act — the coral reef, the 'right whale' lecture, the boat — and notice how Pixar's water simulation (a technical milestone: the light, the current, the physics) makes the ocean the film's real star: the animation was so convincing it won the Oscar. Then watch the ending, where Marlin finally lets Nemo go ('You're free.

name: The Incredibles (2004)
teaser: The superhero film that worked as a family drama — Brad Bird's story of a retired caped crusader (Craig T. Nelson) and his superpowered family, forced back into action. The film's 'No capes!' warning, its midlife-crisis satire, and its baby (Jack-Jack's scene is the decade's funniest animation) made it the best-reviewed film of its year.

exploreAction.targetName: The Incredibles (2004) — the ending and the 'no capes' scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'No capes!' scene — Edna Mode's rant, the montage of superhero deaths — and notice how the film's comedy is its philosophy: the film argues that costumes (and the heroics they imply) kill people, and that real heroism is family.

name: Ratatouille (2007)
teaser: The greatest film ever made about food — Brad Bird's story of Remy, a rat who wants to be a chef in Paris, and the 'anyone can cook' philosophy. The film's critical scene — the food critic Anton Ego's childhood bite of ratatouille, which unlocks his memory — is the decade's most moving single image, and the film won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature.

exploreAction.targetName: Ratatouille (2007) — the Ego scene and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film's final act — the dish, the critic, the flashback — and notice how the film builds to its most famous moment: Ego's bite of ratatouille transports him to his childhood, and the film's argument — that food is memory, and that greatness is a matter of taste, not class — is delivered in that one bite.

name: Inside Out (2015)
teaser: Pixar's most profound film — the story of an 11-year-old girl told from inside her head, where the emotions (Joy, Sadness, Anger, Fear, Disgust) run headquarters. The film's thesis — that sadness is essential, not an enemy — is delivered in the film's most devastating scene (Bing Bong's farewell, 'Take her to the moon for me') and won it the Oscar for Best Animated Feature.

exploreAction.targetName: Inside Out (2015) — the Bing Bong scene and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Bing Bong scene — the imaginary friend, the rocket, the 'take her to the moon for me' — and notice how the film's most famous moment is built from pure emotional mathematics: the character's sacrifice is the film's thesis made literal, and the scene's place in the 'core memory' structure makes it land like a grenade.

name: Toy Story 3 (2010)
teaser: The animated film that made grown adults weep in theaters — Andy's toys, facing the trash heap when their owner goes to college, and the incinerator scene that seemed ready to end them all. It became the first animated film to gross over $1 billion, won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, and its closing act — Andy's slow goodbye, handing his toys to Bonnie — is the most moving ten minutes Pixar has ever made.

exploreAction.targetName: Toy Story 3 (2010) — the incinerator scene and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film's final act — the incinerator, the joined hands, the acceptance — and notice how the film earns its darkness: the toys are facing real death, and their decision to face it together is the film's argument made literal.

name: Frozen (2013)
teaser: The Disney phenomenon that took over the world — two sisters, one ice palace, and 'Let It Go,' the anthem that made Elsa (originally written as the villain until the song changed the story) the most beloved character of the decade. It won 2 Oscars, became the highest-grossing animated film in history at the time ($1.28 billion), and its twist — that the true love that saves Anna is her sister's, not a prince's — quietly modernized the fairy tale.

exploreAction.targetName: Frozen (2013) — 'Let It Go' and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch 'Let It Go' — the ice palace rising, Elsa's transformation — and notice how the song is the film's thesis made spectacle: the animators built a new simulation for the ice, and the sequence's visual freedom (her hair down, her dress changing) is her liberation.

name: Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (2018)
teaser: The superhero film that looked like nothing else — every frame drawn like a comic book panel, with halftone dots, onomatopoeia, and a hero (Miles Morales) who learns that anyone can wear the mask. The animators broke the industry's 'two frames per drawing' rule, drawing each frame individually so the motion feels like a living comic.
byline: Bob Persichetti, Peter Ramsey & Rodney Rothman

exploreAction.targetName: Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (2018) — the leap of faith
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'leap of faith' sequence — Miles stepping off the skyscraper, the music swelling, the dive into the city — and notice how the film earns its most famous moment: the animators studied how spider movements and skateboard physics collide, and the frame's halftone dots and skewed perspectives make the leap feel like a comic page coming alive.

name: Marcel the Shell with Shoes On (2022)
teaser: The most tender film of the decade, and it's about a one-inch-tall shell with one googly eye and tiny shoes — Marcel (voiced by Jenny Slate, in a feature spun off from the viral shorts she created with director Dean Fleischer Camp) lives in an Airbnb and narrates his tiny life: the tennis ball, the lint, the search for his family.

exploreAction.targetName: Marcel the Shell with Shoes On (2022) — the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film's blend of scales — Marcel tiny against real kitchens, the camera peering at him like he's a national treasure — and notice how the film's documentary framing is the joke and the heart: everyone who meets Marcel falls for him instantly, and the film's quiet humor (the '60 Minutes' satire, the group chat) makes room for its real subject.

name: Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse (2023)
teaser: The sequel that outdid the masterpiece — Miles Morales returns, and the film's multiverse of Spider-People (hundreds of them, each in their own animation style) is the most audacious visual experiment in mainstream animation history. The film's first half is a buddy movie, its second half a tragedy about fate, and its cliffhanger ending made audiences scream in theaters.
byline: Joaquim Dos Santos, Kemp Powers & Justin K. Thompson

exploreAction.targetName: Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse (2023) — the chase sequence and the ending
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the chase through the Spider-Society — hundreds of Spider-People, each in their own style, Miles dodging through them — and notice how the film makes its visual language its plot: the different universes are different animation schools colliding, and the chase's changing styles (Indian Spider-Man's watercolor, the Spider-Punk's collages) are the film's argument that no single story is the only one.

name: Monsters, Inc. (2001)
teaser: Pixar's second-biggest idea: monsters scare children for a living because screams power their city. The crew studied real toddler laughter to build the Laugh Floor, and every door in the vault is perspective-exact so the chase works as pure geometry.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Sulley and Mike's friendship against the scare-floor rules, then pay attention to the door chase — the animators made each door's perspective mathematically real so the sequence reads as spatial logic, not magic.

name: Shrek (2001)
teaser: DreamWorks' fairy-tale satire won the first-ever Best Animated Feature Oscar — a category created partly because the studio campaigned so hard against its rival. Mike Myers re-recorded Shrek in a Glaswegian accent after his first take sounded too generic.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film's running argument: fairy-tale rules vs. real feelings. The scene where Shrek mishears Fiona's love as pity is the whole movie in one exchange — and the onion speech lands even harder after it.

name: Shrek 2 (2004)
teaser: The sequel is considered better than the original by many — Puss in Boots was written for Antonio Banderas after a single casting call. The film's fairy-tale-brand satire (Fairy Godmother's 'I Need a Hero') is pure showbiz parody.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a commentary on marriage and insecurity — Fiona's parents' reaction is the plot. The 'I Need a Hero' performance is the movie's thesis: even villains want to be the hero of their own story.

name: How to Train Your Dragon (2010)
teaser: The animators studied real dogs, cats, and horses to build Toothless's body language — and the famous 'no one lands him' scene was the first test of their motion language. The film's flight scenes were rendered with a custom camera rig that made the world feel weightless.

exploreAction.targetName: How to Train Your Dragon (2010) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch Toothless's eyes as the film's entire emotional system — every feeling is telegraphed through pupil movement before a single word. Then notice how the dragon-training scenes teach you the same thing Hiccup learns: dominance fails, trust works.

name: Tangled (2010)
teaser: Tangled's hair took a new software system to simulate — 70,000 individual strands that took 3 days per frame. The studio behind it, Glen Keane, left Disney in 2012 partly because he felt the industry had moved past hand-drawn animation.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the lantern scene as the film's thesis — two people finally seeing each other for real. Then notice how every song in the film is about the same thing: wanting to be seen, not kept.

name: Despicable Me (2010)
teaser: The Minions were originally written as a small army of workers, but the animators loved their gibberish so much they gave them a whole movie to themselves two years later. The film's voice cast included Steve Carell doing a voice he based on a real European accent he heard on vacation.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Gru's arc as a story about earned love — every scheme he runs fails because he's secretly running toward the girls. Then notice the Minions' gibberish: it's actually a blend of several real languages, and the animators tracked which syllables mean what.

name: Wreck-It Ralph (2012)
teaser: The film's game worlds are built from real arcade classics, and the animators studied actual game code to make the film's fictional games feel authentic. The film's tagline, 'Going Turbo,' is a reference to a real arcade legend.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about roles — Ralph's whole arc is learning that he's not defined by his job. Then notice the film's rule: the game worlds have rules, and the film is about what happens when someone breaks them.

name: Big Hero 6 (2014)
teaser: The film's Baymax was designed from a real inflatable robot, and the animators studied actual robotics to make him move like a balloon. The film won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Baymax's movement as the film's emotional center — his 'I will scan you' is a whole character in three words. Then notice the film's San Fransokyo: it's a mashup of two cities that mirrors the film's mashup of heart and tech.

name: How to Train Your Dragon 2 (2014)
teaser: The film's animation was a leap forward — the dragons' fire was simulated with real physics, and the flight scenes used a new camera system. The film's twist, involving Hiccup's mother, was planned from the first film.

exploreAction.targetName: How to Train Your Dragon 2 (2014) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about growing up — Hiccup's arc is about choosing his own path. Then notice the film's message: the dragons' peace is a fragile thing, and the film is about protecting it.

name: The Lego Movie (2014)
teaser: The film was shot entirely in LEGO — every brick is a real LEGO piece, and the animators used actual LEGO sets for reference. The film's twist, that the story is being played by a real boy, was kept secret until release.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about creativity vs. conformity — the Master Builders are the film's thesis. Then notice the film's ending: it's a meditation on play, and the LEGO pieces are the point.

name: Zootopia (2016)
teaser: The film's world is a fully realized animal city, and the animators studied real animals to build the characters — the film's racial allegory was praised by critics. The film won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about prejudice — every character's animal nature is a metaphor for bias. Then notice the film's structure: it's a buddy cop movie where the mystery is the city's own assumptions.

name: Moana (2016)
teaser: The film's ocean was animated with a custom physics system, and the Polynesian culture was researched with real cultural advisors. The film's music was written by Lin-Manuel Miranda, who also wrote the film's title song.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about finding your path — Moana's arc is about the call to the sea. Then notice the film's ocean: it's a character with a personality, and the film's best scenes are the ones where it plays.

name: Kubo and the Two Strings (2016)
teaser: The film was stop-motion — every frame was shot with real puppets, and the film's famous origami scene took 6 months to animate. The film was nominated for two Oscars.

exploreAction.targetName: Kubo and the Two Strings (2016) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about memory — Kubo's music brings the past to life. Then notice the film's craftsmanship: every scene is a hand-made object, and the film's beauty is its message.

name: Onward (2020)
teaser: Pixar's film was inspired by director Dan Scanlon's own loss of his father — the story of two brothers who get one more day with theirs. The film's magic system runs on a visual language of staffs, gems, and spells.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about what you carry from the people you lose — the quest is really about the brothers' relationship. Then notice the film's final act: it's built entirely around a choice that redefines what the quest was for.

name: Encanto (2021)
teaser: Lin-Manuel Miranda's songs for the film were written during quarantine, and 'We Don't Talk About Bruno' became a global phenomenon — it was the first Disney song to top the Billboard Hot 100. The film's setting is a real Colombian style of home.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about family pressure and generational trauma — every member of the Madrigals is crushed by expectation. Then notice the film's house: it's a character, and its crumbling mirrors the family's fractures.

name: Luca (2021)
teaser: The film was inspired by director Enrico Casarosa's childhood summers on the Italian Riviera, and its sea monsters are a metaphor for feeling different. The film's Vespa obsession is a love letter to 1950s Italian culture.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about friendship and belonging — Luca's arc is about being seen for who he is. Then notice the film's design: the Italian town is drawn with the same warmth as the water scenes are drawn with mystery.

name: Raya and the Last Dragon (2021)
teaser: The film's Southeast Asian setting was researched with a cultural team of experts from across the region — the animation includes real martial arts styles from five countries. The film's dragon, Sisu, was voiced by Awkwafina.

exploreAction.targetName: Raya and the Last Dragon (2021) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about trust — Raya's arc is about unlearning her distrust of the world. Then notice the film's message: it's a rare Disney film where the villain's perspective has a point, and reconciliation is the goal.

name: The Mitchells vs. the Machines (2021)
teaser: The film was originally made for theatrical release before the pandemic sent it to Netflix — its distinctive visual style mixes 3D animation with hand-drawn chaos. The film was praised as one of the best animated films of the year.

exploreAction.targetName: The Mitchells vs. the Machines (2021) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about family and technology — the robot apocalypse is a metaphor for the communication gap between parents and kids. Then notice the film's style: it looks like a sketchbook exploded, and that's intentional.

name: Turning Red (2022)
teaser: Pixar's first film directed solely by a woman, Domee Shi's coming-of-age story about a girl who turns into a giant red panda is a metaphor for puberty. The film's 2002 Toronto setting is rich with period detail.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about the messiness of growing up — Mei's panda is her feelings made visible. Then notice the film's honesty: it's a kids' movie that takes a teenager's emotions completely seriously.

name: Lightyear (2022)
teaser: The film is presented as the in-universe movie that inspired the Buzz Lightyear toy — the premise was pitched by Tim Allen's toy in the original Toy Story. Chris Evans voices the human Buzz.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about accepting your mistakes — Buzz's arc is about a failure he can't undo. Then notice the film's framing: the opening text explains the toy connection, and the film honors the character's earnestness.

name: Puss in Boots: The Last Wish (2022)
teaser: The film's animation style was inspired by Spider-Verse's limited-frame look — the stylized rendering was praised as a leap forward for DreamWorks. The film's villain, the Wolf, is a genuinely menacing presence.

exploreAction.targetName: Puss in Boots: The Last Wish (2022) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about mortality — Puss's nine lives are running out, and the film is about facing death. Then notice the film's villain: the Wolf is death itself, and the film's refusal to defeat him is its strength.

name: Pinocchio (2022)
teaser: Guillermo del Toro's stop-motion Pinocchio took 15 years to make and won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature. Del Toro set the story in fascist Italy, making it a meditation on obedience and individuality.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about what it means to be human — Pinocchio's journey is about choosing disobedience over obedience. Then notice the film's politics: the fascist backdrop makes every choice about conformity matter more.

name: The Bad Guys (2022)
teaser: The film's heist-movie structure and stylish animation were praised — the opening heist sequence is a standout. The film is based on the popular children's book series about reformed villains.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about whether people can change — the Bad Guys are trying to be good and failing hilariously. Then notice the film's style: it's a heist movie in animal form, and the action is genuinely slick.

name: Chip 'n Dale: Rescue Rangers (2022)
teaser: The film's premise — the cartoon duo as middle-aged actors in the real world — was praised for its commentary on animation history. The film's cameos include characters from across decades of cartoon copyright law.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about a duo who went their separate ways — the reunion is the film's engine. Then notice the film's visual mix: 2D and 3D animation coexist, and the film uses that to tell its story about the industry.

name: Elemental (2023)
teaser: Pixar's film about fire and water falling in love was drawn from director Peter Sohn's own immigrant family story. The film's cultural specificity — Ember's parents run a corner store — was praised.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about honoring your parents while becoming yourself — Ember's arc is about both. Then notice the film's metaphor: the elements are literal, and the fire-water romance is the whole point.

name: Nimona (2023)
teaser: The film was rescued from Disney's shelving and released by Netflix after its story — a shapeshifter who refuses to be defined — was seen as too queer for the studio. The film was praised as a triumph of adaptation.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about refusing to be the monster they say you are — Nimona's shapeshifting is identity made literal. Then notice the film's villain: the institution that fears difference is the real monster.

name: TMNT: Mutant Mayhem (2023)
teaser: The film's animation style, which looks like hand-drawn teenage sketchbooks, was praised as a fresh take on the franchise — the turtles are voiced by actual teenagers. The film's humor was compared to Spider-Verse.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about being teenagers first and heroes second — the turtles' desire to be accepted is the film's engine. Then notice the film's style: the sketchy animation is a deliberate choice about youth and mess.

name: The Super Mario Bros. Movie (2023)
teaser: The film became one of the highest-grossing animated films ever, despite mixed reviews — it was designed as a love letter to the games, packed with references. Chris Pratt's Mario voice was a controversy before release.

exploreAction.targetName: The Super Mario Bros. Movie (2023) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about family — Mario and Luigi's bond is the emotional core beneath the game references. Then notice the film's craft: it's built to make fans point at the screen, and the references are the plot.

name: Inside Out 2 (2024)
teaser: The sequel added Anxiety, Envy, Embarrassment, and Ennui to Riley's emotional crew — the film's portrayal of an anxiety attack was praised by mental health professionals. It became the highest-grossing animated film ever.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about growing up and the emotions that come with it — Anxiety's arc is about learning to coexist. Then notice the film's ending: the 'self' belief is rebuilt, and the film's message is that feelings are information, not identity.

name: The Wild Robot (2024)
teaser: The film's painterly animation, inspired by the book's illustrations, was praised as a new high for DreamWorks — Roz's journey raising a gosling was an emotional hit. The film was nominated for three Oscars.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about motherhood and belonging — Roz's arc is about becoming something her programming never intended. Then notice the film's visual style: the backgrounds look painted, and the contrast with the robot is the point.

name: Flow (2024)
teaser: The Latvian animated film — a wordless story of a cat surviving a flood — won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature. The film was made with open-source software and no dialogue at all.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story told entirely through movement — the cat's journey is pure visual storytelling. Then notice the film's craft: the animation is stylized, and the film's lack of dialogue makes every sound a character.

name: Memoir of a Snail (2024)
teaser: Adam Elliot's stop-motion film about loneliness and connection won the Oscar for Best Animated Feature — its handcrafted, melancholic style was praised. The film's snail is a metaphor for its protagonist's withdrawn life.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about coming out of your shell — Grace's arc is about letting people in. Then notice the film's craft: it's stop-motion with a handmade soul, and the film's sadness is always warm.

name: Klaus (2019)
teaser: The Netflix animated film was hand-drawn with a new lighting technique — it was praised as a return to classic 2D animation and was nominated for the Oscar. The film reimagines the origin of Santa Claus.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the film as a story about how kindness spreads — every act of generosity in the town creates another. Then notice the film's animation: the hand-drawn style with volumetric lighting is the film's quiet revolution.

name: Anomalisa (2015)
teaser: A customer-service expert who hears everyone as the same voice and face meets a woman whose voice is different, and falls into a brief, strange love. Charlie Kaufman's stop-motion film, with puppets, is the most human movie about loneliness ever animated. It was the first animated film to compete for the Best Picture Oscar.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the hotel-room scene — the film's emotional peak happens between two puppets. Notice how the identical voices make every other character a blur around the one exception.

name: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937)
teaser: The first full-length animated feature ever — critics called it 'Disney's Folly' while it was in production, and it went on to become the highest-grossing film of its era. It took over 200 artists and roughly two years to draw, and its success literally saved the studio and proved animation could carry a feature.

exploreAction.targetName: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the forest flight sequence — the tree branches become grasping hands in the backgrounds, drawn with the multiplane camera for real depth. Then notice how the dwarfs all share one body shape and are told apart purely by personality and color.

name: Pinocchio (1940)
teaser: Disney's second feature won two competitive Oscars — the first animated film to win any — and it nearly bankrupted the studio on release. The animators studied real mine cans and clocks to nail the puppet look, and Jiminy Cricket's 'When You Wish Upon a Star' became Disney's anthem.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening scene where Geppetto's workshop comes alive — every pendulum, cuckoo and music box moves in perfect counter-rhythm. Then watch Monstro the whale: the biggest animated character drawn up to that point.

name: Fantasia (1940)
teaser: The first commercial film released in stereophonic sound — 'Fantasound' used 33 microphones and a 54-speaker setup. Walt Disney lost money on it for years, but it became the template for music-video visuals decades before MTV.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch The Sorcerer's Apprentice with Mickey — it was originally a standalone short, and it's the segment that convinced Disney to expand the film. Then watch the abstract Toccata and Fugue: the music was recorded first, the animation drawn to it.

name: Dumbo (1941)
teaser: Made on a deliberately tiny budget to save the studio after Fantasia's losses — and it became Disney's most profitable feature of the 1940s. The 'Pink Elephants' sequence was drawn with deliberate hallucinogenic logic after the animators decided alcohol logic should drive it.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Pink Elephants parade and notice how the shapes melt into each other with no camera cuts — a full animation tour de force. Then watch the 'Baby Mine' scene, one of the most restrained emotional sequences in Disney history.

name: Bambi (1942)
teaser: The multiplane camera's masterpiece — layered glass plates give the forest real depth, and the backgrounds were painted in a deliberately soft style. The film's hunting-death sequence is the reason conservationists cite a 'Bambi effect' — audiences stopped seeing hunters as heroes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening pan through the forest — the camera travels through painted layers of leaves and trees, the multiplane effect at its peak. Then watch the fire sequence and count how many colors are stripped from the palette as danger closes in.

name: Saludos Amigos (1942)
teaser: A goodwill package film from Disney's 1941 South American tour — the State Department co-funded it to fight Nazi influence in Latin America. It introduced José Carioca and, with it, the studio began treating Latin America as a real market.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Lake Titicaca' segment and note how the animation mixes documentary footage with cartoon Donald. Then watch 'El Gaucho Goofy' — the same Goofy instruction-film formula, now in gaucho gear.

name: The Three Caballeros (1944)
teaser: A psychedelic travelogue before psychedelics — live-action footage meets hand-drawn animation in a splash of color and rhythm. It gave the world the song 'Baía' and the character Panchito Pistoles, and it remains one of Disney's strangest features.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Baía' sequence where live-action Aurora Miranda dances with animated Donald — the blending of film and cartoon was state of the art. Then watch the final surreal gauchito dance and notice how reality keeps dissolving into paint.

name: Make Mine Music (1946)
teaser: A wartime package film of ten music segments — it includes the jazz fable 'Peter and the Wolf' and the surreal 'The Whale Who Wanted to Sing at the Met'. Made to stretch the studio's wartime budget, it proved animation could sell mood, not just story.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch 'The Whale Who Wanted to Sing at the Met' — it's often called the saddest Disney short ever made, a tragedy told in song. Then watch 'Peter and the Wolf' and notice how each character gets its own instrument.

name: Fun and Fancy Free (1947)
teaser: A package film featuring Bongo the bear and a retelling of Jack and the Beanstalk with Mickey, Donald and Goofy — with live-action Edgar Bergen and his dummy Charlie McCarthy hosting. It was the last Disney feature to star Mickey Mouse for over 40 years.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the beanstalk climb: Disney's animators turned the giant Willie into a technical showpiece of scale. Then watch Bongo's story, a musical romance that's essentially a cartoon operetta.

name: Melody Time (1948)
teaser: The last of the wartime package films — seven segments including 'Johnny Appleseed' and a Donald Duck/Goofy double date. Its standout, 'Once Upon a Wintertime', is one of the most beautiful animated scenes of the decade.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch 'Once Upon a Wintertime' — the ice-skating lovers' fall is a masterclass in motion blur and weight. Then watch 'Blame It on the Samba' where Donald meets the Aracuan bird for a rhythm duel.

name: The Adventures of Ichabod and Mr. Toad (1949)
teaser: Two novellas in one: Kenneth Grahame's Wind in the Willows and Washington Irving's Sleepy Hollow — the Headless Horseman chase is one of the scariest sequences Disney ever drew. Bing Crosby narrates the Sleepy Hollow half, improvising his own comic asides.

exploreAction.targetName: The Adventures of Ichabod and Mr. Toad (1949) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Headless Horseman chase in the dark — the animation deliberately breaks into surreal, angular shapes as Ichabod's horse panics. Then rewind and watch Mr. Toad's motorcar madness for the comic counterpart.

name: Cinderella (1950)
teaser: The film that saved Disney's animation department — the studio was deep in debt after the war, and Cinderella's success funded everything that followed. The Fairy Godmother's transformation scene was a technical milestone, and Lucifer the cat is the meanest villain in the classic era.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the transformation scene — the pumpkin-to-coach morph took animators months and is a pure showcase of animated geometry. Then watch Lucifer: every scene he's in, the story is told by his tail and his eyes.

name: Alice in Wonderland (1951)
teaser: Disney's wildest acid-adjacent trip — the Cheshire Cat's face was animated to fade in stages, and the entire film follows dream logic rather than plot. It flopped on release and became a campus favorite in the 1960s counterculture.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Cheshire Cat's first appearance and note how he dissolves part by part — grin, then eyes, then everything. Then watch the Mad Tea Party and try to follow the conversation's rules: there are none.

name: Peter Pan (1953)
teaser: The studio sat on the adaptation for 14 years — Walt bought the rights in 1939. Tinker Bell was animated by Marc Davis and famously modeled on Marilyn Monroe; her glow, and her size (roughly the height of a hand), were drawn with real camera-light tricks.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the flight over London — the multiplane camera dives and banks with the kids. Then watch Tinker Bell's jealousy scene: her face and body language carry the whole plot without a word of dialogue.

name: Lady and the Tramp (1955)
teaser: The first animated feature shot in CinemaScope widescreen — the animators had to rethink every composition for a 2.55:1 frame. The spaghetti kiss was originally rejected as too silly; animator Frank Thomas drew it anyway and the studio kept it.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the spaghetti scene and notice how the camera holds one wide shot for the whole kiss — a composition choice made possible by the new widescreen format. Then watch the rat fight in the nursery: full animal animation, no talking.

name: Sleeping Beauty (1959)
teaser: Shot in 70mm Technirama, drawn in a deliberately angular style inspired by medieval tapestries — the animators hated it at the time and it cost twice its budget. It bombed on release and nearly closed the studio, but its look is now considered the pinnacle of Disney's 'golden' period.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Maleficent's dragon transformation — the horned villain melts into a black dragon in one continuous shot. Then watch the forest of thorns sequence, drawn with sharp verticals that echo the film's tapestried design.

name: One Hundred and One Dalmatians (1961)
teaser: The first Disney feature to use Xerox photocopying — the animators' drawings were transferred directly to cels, keeping pencil texture on screen and cutting cost dramatically. The result was a scratchy, energetic look that saved the studio money and gave the film its identity.

exploreAction.targetName: One Hundred and One Dalmatians (1961) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Twilight Bark' sequence — the message relayed across London by barks is a network story told in silhouette. Then watch Cruella de Vil's car chase: her cigarette smoke, fur coat and car all move in the same manic rhythm.

name: The Sword in the Stone (1963)
teaser: The last Disney feature before Walt's death, and the first where Walt handed most control to a new generation — animator Milt Kahl was reportedly bored and made Merlin's magic feel off-the-cuff. The squirrel-duel scene is still a fan favorite.

exploreAction.targetName: The Sword in the Stone (1963) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the wizard duel between Merlin and Madam Mim — two shapeshifting magicians morphing through animals mid-battle. Then watch the fish scene: the animators drew underwater motion by studying actual carp.

name: The Jungle Book (1967)
teaser: The last animated feature Walt Disney personally supervised — he died during production, and the animators kept his preferred tone of loose, jazzy comedy. The voice cast — Phil Harris, Louis Prima, Sebastian Cabot — was recorded first, and the animation was drawn to their improvisations.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Bear Necessities' number — Baloo's lazy, swinging animation was drawn to Phil Harris's actual singing. Then watch King Louie's 'I Wanna Be Like You': a jazz scat session animated frame by frame around Louis Prima's growls.

name: The Aristocats (1970)
teaser: Disney's last film with its original 'nine old men' era in full force, and the last animated feature approved under Walt's personal style. It's set in 1910 Paris, and the alley-cat 'Everybody Wants to Be a Cat' number is pure jazz improvisation on screen.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the jazz jam at the end — every cat in the alley gets a solo, drawn with real instrument-physicality. Then watch the butler Edgar: his two-thumbed piano gag is a tiny piece of silent-comedy history.

name: Robin Hood (1973)
teaser: Disney reused animation from earlier films to save money — Little John's dance was recycled from Baloo, and Friar Tuck's barrel scene came from The Jungle Book. The recycling gave it a scrappy charm that made it a cult favorite.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Little John and Robin's minstrel-song stroll — the animation is recycled from Baloo and Mowgli, a fact you can feel in the different character proportions. Then watch the archery tournament: the tension is built entirely with close-ups and crowd animation.

name: The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh (1977)
teaser: Three Pooh shorts stitched into a feature — and the first time Pooh's Hundred Acre Wood got the full Disney treatment. The narrator, Sebastian Cabot, appears on screen at the end to close the book, and the storybook pages themselves become part of the scenery.

exploreAction.targetName: The Many Adventures of Winnie the Pooh (1977) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the storybook frame works — characters walk over printed words and the page turns between scenes. Then watch the heffalump dream sequence: it's a full cartoon ballet of bouncing geometry.

name: The Rescuers (1977)
teaser: Bernard and Bianca are the smallest heroes in Disney history — mice running an international rescue society from a UN building, in a box of soap. The film's swamp climax, with its singing villainess Medusa, is one of the darkest scenes in the classic era.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening flight over New York — the city is drawn from a mouse's perspective, everything a hundred times bigger than the heroes. Then watch Medusa's swamp rescue: the mud, the gun, and the alligator make it a proper thriller.

name: The Fox and the Hound (1981)
teaser: Disney's last traditionally-animated feature with its veteran 'nine old men' unit — and the film whose production-era tensions helped push animators like Tim Burton and Don Bluth out of the studio. The hunting-dog betrayal scene is famously tearjerking.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fox and the Hound (1981) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the young-fox scene where Tod first meets Copper — the friendship montage tells a whole childhood in minutes. Then watch the final confrontation: two lifelong friends forced to fight, drawn without a single easy answer.

name: The Black Cauldron (1985)
teaser: Disney's first animated feature with computer-generated imagery — the cauldron itself is CG — and its most expensive flop of the 80s, nearly killing the animation department. It was also Disney's first PG animated feature, and the darkest fairy tale the studio ever drew.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Horned King's army of the dead rise from the cauldron — the film's darkest scene, and the one that got it the PG rating. Then watch the CG cauldron itself: it doesn't match the painted backgrounds, a deliberate first try at the technique.

name: The Great Mouse Detective (1986)
teaser: Disney's first film to use a fully computer-generated scene — the clock-tower fight inside Big Ben was drawn on paper but rendered with early CG for the gears. Basil of Baker Street, the mouse Sherlock Holmes, was inspired by the 1978 Disney TV film The Baker Street Irregulars.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Big Ben climax — the entire clockwork interior is computer-generated, a first for Disney. Then watch Ratigan's death scene: the villain sings 'Goodbye So Soon' while orchestrating his own doom.

name: Oliver & Company (1988)
teaser: Disney's first film set in a modern big city — Oliver Twist retold with dogs and a cat in New York, complete with a Billy Joel theme song. The animators studied real New York streets and real alley-cat body language.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening 'Once Upon a Time in New York City' montage — it's a tour of the city drawn in 1980s neon. Then watch Dodger's 'Why Should I Worry' number: the street choreography turns traffic into a dance floor.

name: The Rescuers Down Under (1990)
teaser: The first Disney animated sequel, and the first feature to use the CAPS digital ink-and-paint system — every frame colored on a computer instead of hand-painted cels. The film's aerial swoop over Australia is one of the most famous tracking shots in animation history.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening eagle flight over the Australian outback — a single continuous camera move that was impossible with hand-inked cels. Then watch Bernard and Bianca: their romance is now fully voiced, and their mousy heroism is on full display.

name: Pocahontas (1995)
teaser: The first Disney animated feature to win two Academy Awards (Best Song and Best Score) for its soundtrack — and the one whose 'Colours of the Wind' became an anthem. The animators studied real Powhatan culture for months, and the film's river sequence is among the most fluid animation Disney ever did.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Colours of the Wind' sequence — the camera circles Pocahontas in one continuous line while the forest comes alive with color. Then watch the final departure: the film's most mature scene, played without villains.

name: The Hunchback of Notre Dame (1996)
teaser: Disney's darkest and most operatic Renaissance-era feature — a musical about lust, faith and social outcasts, adapted from Victor Hugo, complete with a church that sings. 'Hellfire', the villain Frollo's confession, is arguably the boldest song Disney ever put on screen.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hunchback of Notre Dame (1996) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch 'Hellfire' — Frollo's self-justifying duet with a cathedral of fire is a full operatic number. Then watch the Festival of Fools: the crowd animation uses over 20,000 individual character drawings.

name: Hercules (1997)
teaser: A superhero origin story disguised as a Greek myth — the animators modeled the film on sports arenas and gospel choirs, with the Muses as a 1940s girl group. It's the first Disney feature to use the multi-camera CAPS system for a fully digital pan.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the gospel opening number — the Muses tell the whole backstory in one song, a Broadway-style cold open. Then watch the Titans: their design is deliberately stone-and-slab, a contrast to the fluid heroes.

name: Mulan (1998)
teaser: The first Disney princess movie about a woman who saves the country as a soldier — and the first with a Chinese legend at its heart. The film's animators studied Chinese brush painting, and its battle sequence reuses a subtle trick: the Huns' avalanche was drawn with actual snow physics.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the avalanche sequence — the Huns flood the pass, then the snow swallows them in one continuous camera pull. Then watch 'Reflection': the song that launched Lea Salonga's career and made Mulan the first Disney heroine who sings to herself, not to love.

name: Tarzan (1999)
teaser: The first Disney feature where the animators used the 'Deep Canvas' system — a 3D paint engine that lets the camera swoop through trees in real time. The film's tree-surfing is a genuine technical landmark, and Phil Collins wrote the entire score.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the tree-surfing sequence — the camera literally rides the branches through a painted 3D world, a first for Disney. Then watch the gorilla family scenes: the animators studied real mountain gorilla footage for the body language.

name: Fantasia 2000 (1999)
teaser: The sequel to Fantasia, 59 years later — and the first animated film ever released in IMAX. It pairs Rhapsody in Blue with a 1930s New York story, and the finale sets Stravinsky's Firebird on a nature-rebirth myth with a near-silent climax.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Rhapsody in Blue segment — the line drawings of Manhattan swing with Gershwin's syncopation, a love letter to the 1930s. Then watch the Firebird finale: the last five minutes play almost silent, a bold choice for an IMAX spectacle.

name: Dinosaur (2000)
teaser: The first Disney feature to combine live-action backgrounds with fully CG characters — every jungle and rock face is real photography, every dinosaur computer-animated. The iguanodon herd's migration story was the first time Disney made a fully digital epic.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening egg-hatch scene — the baby iguanodon's first steps are pure CG character animation. Then watch the stampede: hundreds of individual dinosaurs, each with its own animation cycle.

name: The Emperor's New Groove (2000)
teaser: A buddy comedy that was almost a dramatic epic called Kingdom of the Sun — Disney threw out a serious Incan story and rebuilt it as a comedy after test screenings. The llama animation is a running gag, and David Spade's Kuzco is a rare Disney protagonist who starts as the villain.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the llama-transformation scene — Kuzco's first words as a llama are a comedy beat that sets the whole tone. Then watch Yzma's poison cabinet: every potion label is a joke, and Eartha Kitt's delivery is pure theater.

name: Atlantis: The Lost Empire (2001)
teaser: Disney's most Jules-Verne-flavored adventure — a 1914 submarine expedition to a lost city, drawn with comic-book energy instead of fairy-tale grace. The film's design, mixing industrial steampunk with Atlantean crystals, was a deliberate break from the Renaissance look.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the submarine descent — the machine's interior is a working steampunk fantasy, all brass and rivets. Then watch Milo's first steps into Atlantis: the city glows with blue crystal light, designed by Mike Mignola of Hellboy fame.

name: Treasure Planet (2002)
teaser: Treasure Island in space — the galleon is a solar-sail ship, the mutiny happens on an asteroid, and the animation mixes hand-drawn characters with fully CG environments. Jim Hawkins' hoverboard surfing is the film's signature image.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Jim's childhood reading of the storybook literally becomes the universe. Then watch the solar-surfing sequence: the boarding scene is a single continuous camera move across a hand-painted galaxy.

name: Brother Bear (2003)
teaser: An Inuit legend about a boy turned into a bear to learn empathy — the first Disney film to use the 'Deep Canvas' paint system for an entire feature. The northern-lights finale was painted with real aurora footage as reference.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the transformation — Kenai's first moments as a bear are told entirely through sound and body language. Then watch the northern lights finale: the aurora was rendered with the same Deep Canvas system that gave Tarzan its tree-surfing.

name: Home on the Range (2004)
teaser: The last traditionally-animated Disney feature before the studio's 2D shutdown — a western about cows who bounty-hunt to save their farm. The film's 'On the Open Range' opening is a full musical number that sets the tone for the movie's classic-Broadway energy.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening number — a musical western with a full chorus, the last of its kind at Disney. Then watch the cattle-rustling climax: the animation team studied real cattle stampedes for the herd movements.

name: Chicken Little (2005)
teaser: Disney's first fully CG feature made outside Pixar — and the first animated movie to use the '3D in a 2D world' look that dominated the next decade. The sky-falling plot is a retelling of the fable with a sci-fi twist.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the alien invasion reveal is the film's big joke, and the animation team spent months on the acorn's physics. Then watch Chicken Little's baseball scene: a full sports-movie climax with an acorn-sized hero.

name: Meet the Robinsons (2007)
teaser: Time-travel comedy about an inventor boy who meets his future family — and the first Disney feature to be shown in Disney Digital 3-D. The film's 'Goob' character was named after the studio's own animation tools, and its message is literally 'keep moving forward'.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the time-jump montage — the future family is introduced in a single chaotic dinner scene that plays like a cartoon musical. Then watch the final reveal: the villain is the boy the hero failed to help, a rare Disney moral twist.

name: Bolt (2008)
teaser: A dog who believes he's a superpowered TV star — the film's 'delusion' joke is that the real world doesn't have stunt doubles. The production studied real border collie footage, and the opening chase sequence is a full action-movie homage.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening chase — Bolt's super-speed is a live-action-style action scene with a dog as the hero. Then watch the RV trip: the film's emotional core is Bolt learning that real life has no cut scenes.

name: The Princess and the Frog (2009)
teaser: Disney's return to traditional hand-drawn animation after a decade of CG — and its first princess movie with a Black lead, Tiana, who wants to open a restaurant, not marry a prince. Set in 1920s New Orleans, it's a jazz musical with a villain who literally feeds on fear.

exploreAction.targetName: The Princess and the Frog (2009) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Tiana's waitress montage tells her whole story through work, and the bayou is painted in the studio's best swamp style since The Rescuers. Then watch the final transformation: the film's love story is earned with a kiss that has to be chosen, not demanded.

name: Winnie the Pooh (2011)
teaser: A return to the storybook style of the 1977 original — the Hundred Acre Wood is drawn in soft watercolor, and the narrator's words become part of the scene again. The film's climax has Pooh and friends literally reading the story's own words to save the day.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how the printed words of the storybook bend, break and become props — a technique the 1977 film pioneered and this one brings back. Then watch the final honey pot sequence: pure slapstick built on a single prop.

name: Frozen II (2019)
teaser: The sequel to the biggest animated film of all time — and the first Disney feature to premiere in 3D and IMAX simultaneously. Its song 'Into the Unknown' was written to sound like a mystery, and the film's real subject is the truth about Elsa's origins, not a villain.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Into the Unknown' sequence — the call-and-answer structure is the film's emotional engine, and the animation team designed the wind as a character. Then watch the autumn forest: the trees were hand-drawn in a new style, mixing 2D and CG.

name: Wish (2023)
teaser: Disney's 100th-anniversary feature — a fairy tale about a girl who wishes on a star, with a villain who hoards wishes. The film mixes hand-drawn and CG animation on purpose, with the backgrounds painted in a watercolor style that evokes the studio's early years.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the watercolor backgrounds and the hand-drawn character animation are deliberately combined, a technical first for Disney. Then watch Star: the wish creature is drawn with real sparkle physics, and its face is a study in pure expression.

name: Moana 2 (2024)
teaser: Originally planned as a Disney+ series, it was reworked into a theatrical feature — and it became one of the biggest animated openings in history. The sequel follows Moana on a voyage to reconnect the ocean's peoples, with new songs by the original team plus new collaborators.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the wayfinding sequences — the animation team consulted real Pacific navigators to make the ocean feel like a living map. Then watch Moana's character design evolve: she's older, stronger, and her journey is now about leading, not just leaving.

name: Toy Story 2 (1999)
teaser: Made twice — the original version was deleted mid-production when a backup failed, and the team rebuilt the film from scratch with a better story. Its 'When She Loved Me' sequence is considered one of Pixar's most emotionally devastating scenes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'When She Loved Me' montage — a single song tells Jessie's entire backstory, with the animation doing the storytelling. Then watch the airport climax: every character's movement is choreographed like a heist movie.

name: A Bug's Life (1998)
teaser: Pixar's second feature, and the first film to use the studio's new 'render farm' — every frame had to be lit like a miniature nature documentary. The grasshoppers' bullying was animated with real biker-gang reference, and the film's hero is a misfit inventor ant, not a warrior.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ant hill scenes — the camera is placed at insect level, and the light is warm and golden like a real meadow. Then watch Hopper's speech: the grasshopper villain's menace is built entirely through slow pacing and stillness.

name: Monsters University (2013)
teaser: A prequel set at a college for monsters — the film's real subject is what happens when your dream doesn't work out. The fraternity rivalry is drawn from the animators' own college stories, and the scare-finale is a full sports-movie climax.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the final scare games — every monster team has its own strategy, and the animation blends fear and comedy in one beat. Then watch Mike's discovery scene: the film's emotional turn, played with no monsters at all, just two friends.

name: Cars (2006)
teaser: Pixar's love letter to Route 66 — the production team drove the actual highway and photographed real diners, motels and gas stations. The film's world, where cars are the only species, is built entirely from automotive references, from tire treads to windshield eyes.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the freeway chase is a full speed-junkie fantasy, with the camera riding the asphalt. Then watch Radiator Springs: every building is a real Route 66 landmark, drawn with the car world's rules.

name: Cars 2 (2011)
teaser: The first Pixar film to become a spy thriller — Mater's bumbling takes him to a world championship in Europe, where every car is a secret agent. The film's espionage plot is played completely straight, which is the joke.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the spy gadgets — every one is car-themed, from tire launchers to oil-slick cannons. Then watch the Tokyo chase: the neon streets were hand-lit with hundreds of individual lights, a Pixar record.

name: Cars 3 (2017)
teaser: A story about aging in the fast lane — Lightning McQueen faces rookies who are faster, and the film's real opponent is time itself. The crash sequence is Pixar's most brutal racing scene, animated with actual crash physics data.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening crash — the impact is rendered with real race-car telemetry, and the sound design does the emotional work. Then watch the final race: the film's twist on mentorship turns the ending into a handoff, not a win.

name: Finding Dory (2016)
teaser: Thirteen years after Finding Nemo, Dory gets her own story — about a fish with short-term memory loss trying to find her parents. The film's climax takes place in a marine institute, and the octopus Hank was animated with a dedicated simulation for each of his seven limbs.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Hank the octopus — every tentacle is individually simulated, and his camouflage scenes are a constant trick of the eye. Then watch the 'speak whale' moment: Dory's best scene, told entirely in whale.

name: Incredibles 2 (2018)
teaser: The sequel that flipped the first film — Bob stays home with the kids while Helen saves the city. It broke the record for biggest animated opening ever, and its 'Dash' speed-running scene is a technical showcase of the studio's new cloth simulation.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the family's new powers are introduced one by one in a montage that doubles as a tutorial. Then watch the babysitter scene: Violet's powers get a full action set piece, and the film's villain is a tech CEO, not a supervillain.

name: Brave (2012)
teaser: Pixar's first fairy tale, and its first film with a female protagonist — Merida, a princess who refuses to be married off. The animators studied real Highland archery, and Merida's hair alone required a dedicated simulation team.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the archery competition — the animation was built around real archer reference, and Merida's form is technically correct. Then watch the bear transformation: the film's central curse turns the story into a mother-daughter bond, not a rescue.

name: Toy Story 4 (2019)
teaser: The fourth Toy Story — and the first Pixar film to win the Best Animated Feature Oscar for a film with a female lead in the key role. The film's real story is about what happens after the adventure: choosing who you want to be, not who you were.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch Forky — a spork who thinks he's trash, animated with a new 'loose' style that lets his parts wobble. Then watch the final decision: the film's ending is a quiet goodbye that rewrites the whole series' logic.

name: The Good Dinosaur (2015)
teaser: The most expensive animated film ever made — its budget reportedly passed $200 million after a complete story redo. It's a western about a gentle dinosaur and a feral human boy, with backgrounds so realistic they were mistaken for live action.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the landscape shots — the rivers, mountains and skies were rendered with photo-real light, a deliberate contrast to the cartoon characters. Then watch the storm sequence: the rain, mud and lightning are all simulated physics.

name: Elio (2025)
teaser: Pixar's sci-fi comedy about a boy mistaken for Earth's ambassador to an alien council. The film's alien designs were inspired by real deep-sea creatures, and its message is about being brave enough to be yourself in a universe that's bigger than you.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the alien council scene — every species has its own body language, designed from real animal reference. Then watch Elio's transformation: the film's emotional beat is a kid learning that 'alien' is just another word for different.

name: The Return of Jafar (1994)
teaser: The first Disney direct-to-video sequel ever — and the one that proved the DTV market existed. It was produced by DisneyToon Studios in under a year, and it launched the Aladdin TV series that followed the film.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the film picks up exactly where Aladdin ended, and the animation budget is visibly leaner than the theatrical original. Then watch the finale: the film's one musical number, 'Forget About Love', is its best moment.

name: Aladdin and the King of Thieves (1996)
teaser: The final chapter of the Aladdin trilogy — Aladdin's father Cassim returns, and the film is about what it means to be a family of thieves. It was the last film in the series before the franchise moved to TV.

exploreAction.targetName: Aladdin and the King of Thieves (1996) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening heist — the Forty Thieves' hideout is a full set-piece, and the animation is a step up from the previous DTV entry. Then watch the final scene: Aladdin's choice between treasure and family is the series' real ending.

name: The Lion King II: Simba's Pride (1998)
teaser: The direct-to-video sequel to the biggest animated film of its era — and one of the few DTV sequels that fans consider a true companion. It tells the Romeo-and-Juliet story of Simba's daughter Kiara and Kovu, a cub from Scar's exiled pride.

exploreAction.targetName: The Lion King II: Simba's Pride (1998) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the film reuses the original's musical language with new songs by the original songwriting team. Then watch Kovu's betrayal scene: the sequel's emotional turning point is a full dramatic beat, rare for a DTV film.

name: The Lion King 1½ (2004)
teaser: The Lion King retold from Timon and Pumbaa's point of view — a comedy that literally watches the original film from the sidelines. Its 'Hakuna Matata' sequence shows the pair's side of events during the famous song.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Timon's childhood in the meerkat colony is a full origin story played for laughs. Then watch the 'Hakuna Matata' sequence: the film shows the original movie happening in the background while the pair do their own thing.

name: The Little Mermaid II: Return to the Sea (2000)
teaser: The DTV sequel about Ariel's daughter Melody, who longs for the sea her mother left behind. Its villain Morgana, Ursula's sister, is the film's best addition — a scheming octopus who speaks with Pat Carroll's signature voice.

exploreAction.targetName: The Little Mermaid II: Return to the Sea (2000) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Melody's birth is the film's emotional anchor, and the animation team reused the original's underwater style. Then watch Morgana's transformation scene: the villain's plan is a mirror of the original, but crueler.

name: The Little Mermaid: Ariel's Beginning (2008)
teaser: A prequel set before the original — Ariel's world before she met Eric, when music was banned in Atlantica. The film is notable for being the last DisneyToon feature with a full theatrical-level song score.

exploreAction.targetName: The Little Mermaid: Ariel's Beginning (2008) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the film's Atlantica is a vibrant underwater kingdom, and the story explains why Ariel loves music so much. Then watch the 'I Will Sing' number: the film's best song, sung by a young Ariel.

name: Cinderella II: Dreams Come True (2002)
teaser: An anthology sequel with three stories — Cinderella's wedding, a castle feast, and Anastasia's redemption. It's the first Cinderella sequel and the first Disney DTV feature to use a fully digital ink-and-paint pipeline.

exploreAction.targetName: Cinderella II: Dreams Come True (2002) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the Anastasia story — the film's best segment, giving the wicked stepsister a genuine character arc. Then watch the wedding story: a full royal-ball sequence animated in the classic Disney style.

name: Cinderella III: A Twist in Time (2007)
teaser: Widely considered the best Disney DTV sequel — the Fairy Godmother's wand is stolen, and the evil stepmother rewrites history so Cinderella never meets the prince. The film's twist is that the prince must remember her, not just recognize her.

exploreAction.targetName: Cinderella III: A Twist in Time (2007) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the wand-stealing scene is a full fairy-tale heist, and the film's premise flips the original's logic. Then watch the climax: Cinderella wins back her own story through memory and identity, a surprisingly modern message for a DTV film.

name: Beauty and the Beast: The Enchanted Christmas (1997)
teaser: A midquel set during the original film's winter — Belle tries to bring Christmas to the castle, and the Beast's rage nearly ruins it. Its villain Forte, a pipe organ who fears change, is one of the most inventive DTV antagonists.

exploreAction.targetName: Beauty and the Beast: The Enchanted Christmas (1997) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch Forte's musical villainy — the organ's chords literally control the castle's mood. Then watch the ice-skating scene: the film's best moment, a duet between Belle and the Beast on the frozen lake.

name: Beauty and the Beast: Belle's Magical World (1998)
teaser: An anthology of three castle-set stories — Belle befriends a misbehaving candelabra, learns the value of books, and faces a rival for the Beast's attention. It's the loosest of the DTV sequels, built from a planned TV series.

exploreAction.targetName: Beauty and the Beast: Belle's Magical World (1998) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 'Fifi' story — the film's warmest segment, about friendship across species. Then watch the library scene: a full song number about the joy of reading, the film's best addition.

name: Pocahontas II: Journey to a New World (1998)
teaser: The sequel sends Pocahontas to London to negotiate peace — a direct-to-video film about diplomacy, not romance. It introduces the real historical figure John Rolfe, and its ending splits from the original's love story.

exploreAction.targetName: Pocahontas II: Journey to a New World (1998) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the London arrival — the animation team drew real Elizabethan architecture, and the film's fish-out-of-water comedy lands. Then watch the final scene: Pocahontas chooses her people and her own future, a rare agency for a princess sequel.

name: Mulan II (2004)
teaser: The DTV sequel about Mulan's wedding — Shang is ordered to escort three princesses to a political marriage, and Mulan must decide what she believes in. It's a film about duty versus love, told with the original's voice cast.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the convoy journey — the film's best scenes are the debates between Mulan and Shang over honor. Then watch the finale: Mulan chooses her own path, and the film ends with a wedding that's earned, not arranged.

name: Tarzan II (2005)
teaser: A midquel set between the original's first act — a young Tarzan, rejected by the gorillas, runs away and meets a creature like himself. Its antagonist, a monstrous 'Zugor', is voiced by a comedic actor playing a false legend.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the jungle — the film's animation is a step up from most DTV sequels, with the Deep Canvas backgrounds returning. Then watch the 'Who Am I' number: the film's emotional song, sung by a Tarzan who's learning his own worth.

name: Bambi II (2006)
teaser: A midquel set after Bambi's mother's death — the Great Prince must raise his son, and neither knows how. It was the first DisneyToon sequel to use the original film's visual style, and its 'There is Life' sequence is a full musical set piece.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the father-son dynamic — the Great Prince's training montage is the film's heart, and the animation matches the 1942 original's soft palette. Then watch the winter sequence: the film's emotional climax, played without words.

name: The Hunchback of Notre Dame II (2002)
teaser: The DTV sequel about Quasimodo's heart — he falls for a circus girl while Frollo's ghost story haunts the city. It's a lighter film than the original, with a clock-tower love story at its center.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hunchback of Notre Dame II (2002) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the film reuses the original's Paris setting, and the animation is a clear step down from the theatrical. Then watch the finale: Quasimodo's bell-ringing, the character's one true language, gets a full musical moment.

name: The Fox and the Hound 2 (2006)
teaser: A midquel set during the friends' childhood — Tod and Copper meet a singing dog group, the Singin' Strays, and Copper must choose between the band and his best friend. Its country-music soundtrack was produced in Nashville.

exploreAction.targetName: The Fox and the Hound 2 (2006) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the country-fair scenes — the film's best moments are the singing dog band's performances. Then watch Copper's choice: the sequel's emotional core is a friendship tested by fame.

name: Lady and the Tramp II: Scamp's Adventure (2001)
teaser: The DTV sequel about Lady and Tramp's rebellious son Scamp, who longs to run with the junkyard dogs. Its love story with Angel is a direct echo of his parents' original — and the film's 'Junkyard Society' song is a full ragtime number.

exploreAction.targetName: Lady and the Tramp II: Scamp's Adventure (2001) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the junkyard scenes — the feral dogs' world is the film's best design, a chaotic contrast to the tidy house. Then watch the finale: Scamp learns that home and freedom aren't opposites.

name: 101 Dalmatians II: Patch's London Adventure (2003)
teaser: The DTV sequel where Patch, the spotted oddball, gets to be a hero alongside his TV idol Thunderbolt. It's a film about finding your own spot — literally, in a world of identical dogs.

exploreAction.targetName: 101 Dalmatians II: Patch's London Adventure (2003) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the TV-show sequence — Patch's fantasy life as a hero is animated in the Thunderbolt cartoon style. Then watch the finale: the film's best gag, a fake-out involving paint, puts Patch at the center of the rescue.

name: Return to Never Land (2002)
teaser: The sequel about Wendy's daughter Jane, who doesn't believe in Peter Pan until the pirates take her. It's the first Disney feature to use the CAPS digital system from start to finish, and its animation keeps the 1953 original's round, warm style.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the flight scenes — the animation team rebuilt the 1953 London look with modern digital tools. Then watch the final duel: Hook's defeat is a full action set piece, and Jane's belief is the weapon.

name: The Jungle Book 2 (2003)
teaser: The DTV sequel about Mowgli's life in the man-village — he misses the jungle, and Baloo comes to get him. It's the first DisneyToon sequel with a full theatrical voice cast, including Haley Joel Osment as Mowgli.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the village scenes — the film contrasts Mowgli's two worlds through light and color. Then watch the final chase: Baloo and Mowgli's escape from Shere Khan is a full jungle run, animated with the original's loose energy.

name: Stitch! The Movie (2003)
teaser: The first of the Lilo & Stitch TV movies — Stitch must track down the other experiments Jumba created before an alien bounty hunter does. It launched the series Lilo & Stitch: The Series, and its cliffhanger ending was designed for TV.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the experiment reveal — every new alien is a one-joke character with its own power. Then watch the finale: Stitch's choice to protect his new family is the franchise's emotional core, played for both comedy and heart.

name: Lilo & Stitch 2: Stitch Has a Glitch (2005)
teaser: A midquel set between the original film and its series — Stitch's programming glitches out at the worst moments. The film's final scene reuses the original's 'Aloha ʻOe' farewell, a deliberate echo of the first movie's ending.

exploreAction.targetName: Lilo & Stitch 2: Stitch Has a Glitch (2005) end-to-end
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the glitch scenes — Stitch's malfunctions are played for comedy first, then tragedy as the stakes climb. Then watch the finale: the film's climax is a quiet, emotional decision, a rarity for a DTV sequel.

name: Leroy & Stitch (2006)
teaser: The series finale that wraps up the Lilo & Stitch story — the evil Dr. Hamsterviel clones Stitch into an army of Leroy. It's the last Disney animated film produced for television before the studio's DTV division closed.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the film's recap of the series is a full musical montage. Then watch the finale: Lilo's family, the experiments and the whole island come together for the franchise's true ending.

name: Atlantis: Milo's Return (2003)
teaser: The DTV sequel that completes the Atlantis story — Milo and his crew face three new threats to the lost city, adapted from the planned TV series. It's a series of adventures rather than one story, and its animation is a step down from the theatrical.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the kraken sequence — the film's most complete action set piece, with the sub crew at full power. Then watch the finale: the Atlantean crystal's secret is revealed, closing the loop the theatrical film opened.

name: Brother Bear 2 (2006)
teaser: The DTV sequel about Kenai's past — he must reunite with his childhood friend Nita, who is being forced to marry. It's a film about memory and love, and its 'Welcome to This Day' song is its emotional anchor.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the film flashes back to Kenai's human life, and the animation matches the original's painted style. Then watch the finale: Kenai's choice between his bear life and his past is the sequel's true subject.

name: Kronk's New Groove (2005)
teaser: The Emperor's New Groove sequel told from Kronk's perspective — the villain-turned-chef wants to impress his father. It's a comedy about self-worth, and its opening song 'A Little More' is a full Broadway-style number.
